title: The purpose of a loading dose

segs.text: Module three, objective five. Why a loading dose is given. An infusion alone takes three to five half-lives to approach C s s, its steady state concentration, so the patient sits below the target for that time. A loading dose, D L, is an I V bolus that puts in at once the amount of drug the infusion would take that long to build up. So C p, the plasma concentration, reaches C s s almost immediately, and the infusion, at its rate R, then only has to replace what is eliminated each hour. She said, the loading dose helps us to reach that steady state concentration, like almost immediately.

card.m: infusion alone: 3 to 5 half-lives below target
C<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>ss</sub> almost at once; R replaces what leaves

segs.text: The loading dose changes when the target is reached, and nothing else. The plateau is R over clearance, and the dose is not in it, so the level the patient is held at is set by the infusion rate. The half-life depends on the clearance and V D, the apparent volume of distribution, so the loading dose does not change it either. The textbook adds the other side: a loading dose reaches the target quickly but cannot hold it, which needs the right infusion rate, and a higher infusion rate gives a higher plateau, not an earlier arrival at the same one.

card.m: C<sub>ss</sub> = {{frac:R|Cl}}: set by R, not by D<sub>L</sub>
D<sub>L</sub> reaches the target; R holds it
higher R: higher plateau, same time

segs.text: When D L is chosen correctly, the falling bolus curve and the rising infusion curve add to a flat line at C s s; adding the two at the same time is called superposition. Too large a loading dose starts the level above the plateau, and it falls to it. Too small a loading dose starts the level below the plateau, and it rises to it, though sooner than with no loading dose at all. The plateau itself is set by the infusion. She said, you got to choose wisely on the loading dose.

card.m: bolus falls + infusion rises = flat at C<sub>ss</sub>
superposition: add the two at the same time
D<sub>L</sub> too large: starts above, falls to C<sub>ss</sub>
D<sub>L</sub> too small: starts below, rises to C<sub>ss</sub>, sooner than with none

segs.text: C p is the bolus part plus the infusion part: D L over V D times e to the minus k t, plus C s s times one minus e to the minus k t, with k the fraction eliminated per hour. Rearranged, C p equals C s s plus the difference between the starting level, D L over V D, and C s s, times e to the minus k t. If the starting level equals C s s, the difference is zero and C p is C s s at every time. If it is larger, the difference is positive and shrinks by first order, so the level falls to the plateau; if it is smaller, the difference is negative and the level rises to it.

card.m: C<sub>0</sub> > C<sub>ss</sub>: falls to it; C<sub>0</sub> < C<sub>ss</sub>: rises to it

segs.text: Her slide Example eight: a two hundred eighty eight milligram loading dose is given with an infusion of fifty milligrams per hour, the half-life is four hours, V D is twelve liters, and the question asks C p at two and at four hours. The sum of the two parts answers it, and it shows whether this dose holds the plateau. k comes from the half-life: zero point one seven three two five per hour. The bolus part starts at twenty four milligrams per liter and has fallen to sixteen point nine seven by two hours. The plateau of the infusion is twenty four point zero five milligrams per liter, and by two hours the infusion part has reached seven point zero four.

card.m: D<sub>L</sub> = 288 mg, R = 50 mg/hr, t<sub>½</sub> = 4 hr, V<sub>D</sub> = 12 L

segs.text: In Example eight, bolus part plus infusion part is twenty four milligrams per liter at two hours, the same as the plateau. Four hours is one half-life, so the bolus part is half of twenty four and the infusion part half of the plateau, and the sum is again twenty four. It stays flat because the dose matches the amount held at steady state: R over k is two hundred eighty eight point six milligrams. She said, We want the loading dose to look like the amount of drug that's in the body at steady state. In class she reworked it with three hundred eighty eight milligrams: the level started above the plateau of twenty four and was about thirty milligrams per liter at two hours, still falling toward it.

Her graded quiz asked, Why is a loading dose used? The keyed answer is to immediately obtain a therapeutic plasma concentration; reducing adverse effects, improving adherence and reducing the half-life are wrong, because a loading dose changes when the target is reached, not the half-life and not the plateau. As a one sentence answer: the loading dose puts in at once the amount that would otherwise take three to five half-lives to accumulate. A renal failure part asks how long a new steady state takes; it is counted in the new, longer half-lives, four point three two of them for ninety five percent in her Practice three. Objective four gives the two routes to the dose itself.

card.m: ✓ to immediately obtain a therapeutic C<sub>p</sub>
wrong: adverse effects, adherence, a shorter t<sub>½</sub>
D<sub>L</sub>: at once, what takes 3 to 5 half-lives
renal failure: 95% at 4.32 of the new, longer half-lives
